title: How to Handle Tax and VAT Data When You Source Through Syncee Suppliers
excerpt: Syncee suppliers ship from different countries, which changes who owes tax and what paperwork you need. This walkthrough covers the fields to capture per product and per invoice.
body: Sourcing through a supplier marketplace means your tax position changes product by product. A Syncee catalog can mix a supplier registered in one country with a warehouse in another, and what applies depends on where goods ship from, where they land, and whether you are registered in that market. Most new sellers discover the gap at year end, when invoices do not match payouts and nobody can say which orders created which obligation. The fix is boring and cheap: capture the right fields at the moment you list the product, not twelve months later.

For every product you push to your store, record supplier country, ship from country, unit cost, and whether the supplier price includes tax. Those four fields decide almost every downstream question. A supplier price that includes value added tax is not comparable to one that excludes it, and mixing the two makes your margin report wrong even when your sales report is right. Keep the fields in the product record rather than in a spreadsheet on one laptop, because the listing is the thing that survives staff turnover.

Then separate what you collect from what you remit. At checkout you collect tax based on your store registrations and the destination rules you configured. On the supplier invoice you pay tax based on the supplier location and their registration. Those two numbers are not supposed to match, and forcing them to match is how people end up claiming input tax they never paid. Reconcile monthly: tax collected by market, tax paid on supplier invoices, and the difference, with a note on any market where that difference swings more than expected.

Marketplace and facilitator rules add a second layer. In several markets the platform that facilitates the sale is treated as the seller for tax purposes, so your store remits on some orders while a marketplace remits on others. Check the rule for each market you actually ship to, write it beside the registration threshold, and review it twice a year. Thresholds move, and crossing one without noticing turns a profitable quarter into a filing problem. If you sell into the European Union or the United Kingdom, get a professional to confirm the setup before your first large quarter.

Build a monthly pack and stop improvising. One folder per month holding the store tax report, the supplier invoice export, the payout statement, and a short note on anything unusual. Name files with year and month so they sort correctly, and keep them for the retention period your accountant gives you, which is usually several years. The pack takes twenty minutes if the fields were captured at listing time and two days if they were not. That difference is the entire argument for doing this early.

The trigger to register, the trigger to file, and the trigger to panic are three different things, and only the first two belong on your calendar. Write down your registration triggers per market, check them monthly against shipped volume, and set a reminder before each filing deadline. None of this makes tax interesting, but it keeps a supplier marketplace from becoming an accounting surprise. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and /tool/syncee lists the supplier data worth capturing before you publish.
